summary.case_overview: This is a constitutional reference before a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court of India to determine whether the right to privacy is recognized as a fundamental right under the Constitution of India [Page 569] [Page 876]. The Court examined the historical backdrop, international covenants, constitutional provisions in Part III, and previous precedents, specifically addressing the correctness of earlier judgments in M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh [Page 569] [Page 709]. The bench delivered concurrent and separate opinions holding that the right to privacy is an inalienable natural right intrinsic to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and other freedoms guaranteed in Part III of the Constitution [Page 573] [Page 920].
summary.facts_of_case: The matter arose from Writ Petition (Civil) No. 494 of 2012 filed by Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) and another against the Union of India and others, challenging the Aadhaar card scheme promoted by the Government of India on the ground that the collection of demographic and biometric data violates the right to privacy [Page 569] [Page 583]. During the proceedings, the correctness of the foundational rulings in M.P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra and Kharak Singh v. State of U.P.—which had held that the Indian Constitution does not protect a right to privacy—was referred to a larger bench [Page 569] [Page 583]. A nine-judge bench was constituted under Article 145(3) to settle the constitutional question [Page 579].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the right to privacy is guaranteed as a fundamental right under the Constitution of India, either as part of Article 21 or within the freedoms enumerated in Part III [Page 569] [Page 573]. Whether the previous judgments in M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh correctly stated that the right to privacy is not protected under the Indian Constitution [Page 569] [Page 573].
summary.important_arguments_or_content: The petitioners, supported by various senior counsel including Shri Soli Sorabjee, Shri Gopal Subramanium, Shri Shyam Divan, Shri Arvind Datar, Shri Anand Grover, Shri Sajan Poovayya, Ms. Meenakshi Arora, Shri Kapil Sibal, Shri P.V. Surendranath, and Ms. Aishwarya Bhati, submitted that privacy is a natural, inalienable, and primordial right that inheres in every human being and is an essential facet of personal liberty, dignity, and autonomy under Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution [Page 572] [Page 577] [Page 946]. Conversely, the Attorney General of India, Shri K.K. Venugopal, along with other counsel appearing for respondents and intervenors such as Shri Tushar Mehta, Shri Aryama Sundaram, Shri Rakesh Dwivedi, Shri Arghya Sengupta, Shri Jugal Kishore, and Shri Gopal Sankaranarayanan, contended that the framers of the Constitution deliberately avoided including a general right to privacy or a 'due process' clause, that privacy is at best a common law or statutory right rather than a fundamental right, and that foundational claims to privacy should not override pressing state concerns such as the distribution of welfare benefits under the Aadhaar framework or take precedence over the right to life of impoverished citizens [Page 850] [Page 876].
summary.court_reasoning: The Court reasoned that fundamental rights are natural and inalienable rights that pre-exist the Constitution and are merely recognized and protected by it [Page 577] [Page 719]. The expression 'personal liberty' under Article 21 and the freedoms in Part III cannot be read in water-tight compartments; rather, they form a rational continuum where privacy serves as an essential condition precedent and core enabler for the exercise of individual autonomy, dignity, and freedom [Page 575] [Page 657] [Page 938]. M.P. Sharma did not adjudicate upon whether privacy emanates from Article 21 or other provisions of Part III, and Kharak Singh's majority holding denying privacy was illogical and contrary to constitutional interpretation [Page 569] [Page 573]. Dignity and privacy are inextricably intertwined, securing the inner recesses of human personality, family, sexual orientation, and informational self-determination [Page 570] [Page 578]. Furthermore, like other fundamental freedoms, privacy is not absolute and any state encroachment must satisfy a three-fold requirement: (i) legality (existence of a valid law), (ii) legitimate state aim, and (iii) proportionality ensuring a rational nexus between objects and means [Page 571] [Page 992].
summary.decision_or_conclusion: The Supreme Court unanimously concluded that: (i) The decision in M.P. Sharma holding that the right to privacy is not protected by the Constitution stands overruled; (ii) The decision in Kharak Singh to the extent that it holds that the right to privacy is not protected by the Constitution stands overruled; (iii) The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution; and (iv) Subsequent decisions recognizing privacy lay down the correct position in law [Page 598] [Page 599]. The cases are sent back to the original three-judge bench for adjudication on merits [Page 573] [Page 920].
summary.important_legal_provisions: Constitution of India - Articles 12, 14, 19, 20(3), 21, 25, 29, 32, 145(3), 368; Preamble to the Constitution of India; Universal Declaration of Human Rights, 1948 (Article 12); International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, 1966 (Article 17); Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (Section 2(1)(d)) [Page 571] [Page 572] [Page 579] [Page 911].
summary.simplified_explanation: The Supreme Court decided whether people in India have a fundamental constitutional right to privacy [Page 569] [Page 583]. The Court ruled that privacy is a natural, essential human right that belongs to every individual and is safely tucked inside the right to life and personal liberty (Article 21) as well as other fundamental freedoms guaranteed by the Constitution [Page 572] [Page 573] [Page 577]. This means the government cannot arbitrarily intrude into a person's home, private choices, sexual orientation, or personal data without a fair law that serves a legitimate state purpose and meets the test of proportionality [Page 571] [Page 578]. Older court judgments which stated that India's Constitution does not protect privacy were formally overruled [Page 569] [Page 573].
summary.limitations: This summary is strictly limited to the legal questions addressed by the nine-judge bench regarding the existence of the fundamental right to privacy and the overruling of M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh, and does not evaluate the final merits of the Aadhaar challenge [Page 573] [Page 876].
